_scope: Every Statistics Canada product named by SOR/2007-303 that has no node to point at. One lead per missing publication, with the provisions that name it and a verbatim quote. Creates no edges — the cluster is blocked on node coverage, not on evidence. Companion to equalization-payroll-base.json, which took the two edges whose targets already exist.

_dropped.why: The single highest-value missing node in this cluster, because it is named in the DIVISION 1 definitions that apply to all ten provinces rather than in the Nova Scotia division. SOR/2007-303 s. 3.1, definition of household final consumption expenditures: 'household final consumption expenditures as determined by Statistics Canada for the purpose of its Provincial and Territorial Economic Accounts, net of any taxes on products, also as determined by Statistics Canada'. The same section pins two housing components to it: 'residential renovations as determined by Statistics Canada for the purpose of its Provincial and Territorial Economic Accounts' and 'residential housing transfers as determined by Statistics Canada for the purpose of its Provincial and Territorial Economic Accounts'. Also named at s. 8(1)(z.2) for the Nova Scotia division: 'household disposable income in the province for the calendar year that ends in the fiscal year, as determined by Statistics Canada for the purpose of its Provincial and Territorial Economic Accounts'. Note the construction 'for the purpose of its X' throughout — the Regulations do not merely cite a number, they adopt Statistics Canada's definition of it for a named product, which is why these are definitional and apply to every province's revenue base at once.

Named in the DIVISION 1 definitions at s. 3.1 and again in the Nova Scotia division, and it cites the tables down to the individual matrix. From s. 3.1, capital expenditures: 'expenditures on commodities, as determined by Statistics Canada for the purpose of its Provincial Supply and Use Tables’ summary level final demand matrix'. And intermediate input expenditures: 'expenditures on intermediate inputs, as determined by Statistics Canada for the purpose of its Provincial Supply and Use Tables’ summary level intermediate input matrix'. At s. 8(1)(z): 'the current dollar gross domestic product at factor cost in the province for the calendar year that ends in the preceding fiscal year … as determined by Statistics Canada on the basis of data from its Provincial Supply and Use Tables'. Naming a matrix inside a table inside a programme is the finest-grained citation in the corpus so far, and it sharpens the release-versus-series question rather than answering it. Related to but distinct from the national Supply, Use and Input-Output Tables lead in statcan-macro-accounts.json — that one is IMDB record 1401 at the national level, this one is the provincial and territorial tables.

_dropped.edge: fiscal-equalization-program -> (System of Macroeconomic Accounts, as a framework)
_dropped.why: The most frequently named product in the Regulations and the one this graph is least able to represent. Named in the DIVISION 1 definitions at s. 3.1 three times over, for the three capital-formation aggregates: 'gross fixed capital formation in intellectual property products, as determined by Statistics Canada on the basis of data for or from its System of Macroeconomic Accounts'; 'gross fixed capital formation in machinery and equipment, as determined by Statistics Canada on the basis of data for or from its System of Macroeconomic Accounts'; 'gross fixed capital formation in non-residential structures, as determined by Statistics Canada on the basis of data for or from its System of Macroeconomic Accounts'. And in the DIVISION 1 revenue base at s. 5(b)(i): 'the portion of the aggregate of corporate profits in Canada, before the payment of income taxes and without any deduction of the aggregate of corporate losses in Canada, that is attributable to any of the 10 provinces for the calendar year that ends in the fiscal year, as determined by Statistics Canada for the purpose of its System of Macroeconomic Accounts'. The CSMA is an accounting framework, not a release with a cadence, so it cannot become a node under the current model — but four separate revenue-base components depend on it definitionally, so leaving it unrepresented understates the Equalization Program's real input set. This is the same problem as the statcan-hfce / statcan-national-accounts duplication and the same problem as bea-gdp -> bea-pce, arriving from a third direction. THREE THINGS ARE NOW BLOCKED ON ONE DECISION: whether a node may be a named series or framework rather than a release.

Upgrades the lead already recorded in equalization-payroll-base.json from the territorial provision to the DIVISION 1 all-provinces revenue base, which is a materially stronger citation. SOR/2007-303 s. 5(b)(ii): 'as determined on the basis of data prepared by Statistics Canada for the purpose of the Government Finance Statistics'. Also at s. 19(1)(b)(ii) for Territorial Formula Financing. Worth building because imf-gfsm — the IMF manual the Canadian programme implements — is already a node, so this would complete a chain from a statutory transfer formula through a national statistical programme to an international standard, which is the shape the international cluster currently lacks.

Seven occurrences in s. 8, more than any other named survey in the section, across the oil, heavy oil, mined oil, natural gas and volume-based revenue bases. Representative, s. 8(1)(p): 'in the case of mined oil revenues described in paragraph 7(1)(p), the total value of the marketable production of synthetic petroleum from hydrocarbon deposits in the province in the calendar year that ends in the fiscal year, as determined by Statistics Canada on the basis of its survey Oil and Gas Extraction'. The survey also carries the statutory definitions of value of oil at s. 8(4) and value of natural gas at s. 8(6). CITATION CORRECTION: those two definitions were reported as sitting at s. 8(3) and s. 8(5); they are in s. 8(4) and s. 8(6), which are the subsections defining the terms used in (3) and (5). One subsection out. Of direct interest because the corpus already has a dense Alberta energy-royalty cluster whose valuation runs through NYMEX WTI, ICE Brent and Argus, and this is the federal statistical measure of the same physical production.

_dropped.edge: fiscal-equalization-program -> (R.L. Polk & Co., Canadian and International Registration Manual)
_dropped.why: A commercial publication named verbatim in a federal regulation, which is the exact shape the V0.5 commercial-source decision was written for. SOR/2007-303 s. 8(1)(i): 'the aggregate, over the following categories of vehicles, of the number of registered vehicles in each category, as determined by Statistics Canada for the purpose of CANSIM table 405-0004, Road motor vehicles, registrations, multiplied by the weighted average licence fee for that category over all provinces, as calculated on the basis of data respecting licence fees charged by each province contained in the R.L. Polk & Co. publication Canadian and International Registration Manual'. Note the regulation says 'the R.L. Polk & Co. publication' — it is a published, titled, recurring commercial product, so it qualifies as a node under the same rule that admits J.D. Power and ICE Brent, and unlike Haver Analytics it publishes something of its own. This was found while checking the alcoholic-beverage rows and was not in the returned research; it is the third commercial source found sitting inside a government funding formula, after J.D. Power in the US CPI and ICE Brent in Alberta's bitumen valuation.

_dropped.edge: fiscal-equalization-program -> (CANSIM table 405-0004, Road motor vehicles, registrations)
_dropped.why: Named twice, at s. 8(1)(h) and s. 8(1)(i), for the non-commercial and commercial motor vehicle licensing revenue bases. From s. 8(1)(h): 'the sum of the following numbers in the province in the calendar year that ends in the fiscal year, each as determined by Statistics Canada for the purpose of CANSIM table 405-0004, Road motor vehicles, registrations, or by the Minister if Statistics Canada does not make the determination'. The trailing clause is worth keeping: the regulation provides for the Minister to substitute if Statistics Canada stops producing the table, which is the second statutory fallback-for-a-discontinued-source found in this corpus after the Oil Sands Royalty Regulation's provision for the day the Bank of Canada stops publishing an exchange rate.

_dropped.edge: fiscal-equalization-program -> (CANSIM table 002-0020, Balance sheet of the agricultural sector)
_dropped.why: SOR/2007-303 s. 8(1)(z), the property-tax revenue base: 'the value of farm land in the province, measured in current dollars as of the end of the calendar year that ends in the preceding fiscal year, as determined by Statistics Canada for the purpose of CANSIM table 002-0020, Balance sheet of the agricultural sector, at December 31, and ratios'. Note this is the Nova Scotia division's farm measure, where the Territorial Formula Financing parallel at s. 19(1)(h) uses the Census of Agriculture instead — two divisions of one regulation measuring farm value from two different StatCan products.

_dropped.edge: fiscal-equalization-program -> (table 23-10-0066-01, Sales of fuel used for road motor vehicles)
_dropped.why: SOR/2007-303 s. 1(1), in the general Interpretation section rather than a revenue base, defining the fuel quantities used throughout: 'as determined by Statistics Canada for the purpose of table 23-10-0066-01, Sales of fuel used for road motor vehicles, annual (× 1,000)'. Cited with the modern table number, unlike the CANSIM-era citations elsewhere in the same instrument — see the vintage note below.

SOR/2007-303 s. 8(1)(z.1): 'in the case of race track taxes described in paragraph 7(1)(z.1), the gross amount wagered in the province in the calendar year that ends in the fiscal year at pari-mutuel tracks on harness and running horse races, as determined by the Canadian Pari-Mutuel Agency'. Agency named, no publication named, and no recurring titled release identified. Filed as unpublishable rather than as a lead so that a later pass does not treat it as researchable — if a CPMA publication does turn out to exist this can be reclassified, but on the regulation's wording alone there is nothing to point at.

_dropped.edge: SOR/2007-303 — table-number vintages disagree between divisions
_dropped.why: A corpus fact that will matter when these nodes are built. The same instrument cites Statistics Canada tables under two incompatible numbering systems, split by division. The Nova Scotia division uses retired CANSIM numbers: s. 8(1)(j) cites 'CANSIM table 183-0024, Sales of alcoholic beverages by volume, value and per capita 15 years and over, fiscal years ended March 31' for spirits, wine and beer in three separate subparagraphs; s. 8(1)(z) cites 'CANSIM table 002-0020'; s. 8(1)(h) and (i) cite 'CANSIM table 405-0004'. The Territorial Formula Financing part uses the current numbering for the same subject matter: s. 19(1)(f) cites 'table 10-10-0011-01, Value of sales of alcoholic beverages of liquor authorities and other retail outlets, by beverage type (× 1,000)' for the same three beverages. And the general Interpretation at s. 1(1) uses the current numbering too, at 'table 23-10-0066-01'. CANSIM was retired in favour of the current product-identifier scheme around 2018, so DIVISION 2 is citing tables under numbers Statistics Canada no longer publishes under. Two consequences. Any node built from a CANSIM citation has to be matched to its modern successor by hand, and that match is a judgement, not a quotation. And it corroborates the scope caveat on the SEPH edge: DIVISION 2 was not revised when the rest of the instrument was, which is consistent with its role as a legacy calculation for the Nova Scotia accords rather than a live all-provinces formula.

_dropped.edge: SOR/2007-303 — which division each citation lives in
_dropped.why: Recorded because a section number alone hides it, and it determines how much any of this is worth. Of the twenty-four provisions returned in this round, twelve sit in s. 8 — DIVISION 2 — Nova Scotia, which defines revenue base 'For the purpose of sections 3.71 to 3.9 of the Act', the Nova Scotia additional-equalization provisions, and retains the pre-2007 thirty-three-source revenue structure with paragraphs running (a) to (z.5). Ten sit in s. 3.1 and s. 5, which are DIVISION 1 — Fiscal Equalization to the Provinces, the live all-provinces formula with five revenue sources. Two sit in the general Interpretation at s. 1(1). THE DIVISION 1 CITATIONS ARE THE VALUABLE ONES and they are the minority. The s. 3.1 definitions in particular are what makes Tier 2's thesis true as originally stated — every province's revenue base runs through the same handful of named products — because they are definitions and not per-province measurements. The s. 8 citations are real, verified and narrower than they look. Also worth noting on packaging: the s. 3.1 definitions carry no paragraph numbers of their own, being definitions in an interpretation section, so they are citable only as 's. 3.1, definition of X'. That is the correct answer for them and is what NO CITABLE LOCATION was meant to elicit.
